summary: A sales coaching one-to-one that opens with a formal performance warning and then becomes a detailed pitch teardown. Chris Klevan tells Richard his close rate is well below the 20% KPI — around 11% by another manager's count — and sets an explicit condition: reach 20% by the end of the week or be moved to lower priority on the calendar, with a further conversation about his position if that does not work, noting that paid ads make unconverted calls a direct cost. They then review the call Richard had just finished, lost to a prospect living off savings who had expected $199 a month. Chris's central coaching is that Richard's pitch is feature-led and generic, and must become a customised transformation narrative built from what discovery surfaced; he models a full pre-pitch verbatim, introduces a bridge-and-safari-guide metaphor, and instructs Richard to stop reading from the pitch document. He also renames the third pillar from 'support and accountability' to 'lifelong success'.
notable: Explicit close-rate KPI and performance ultimatum on record: 'Close rates quite a bit under KPI... If by the end of this week, we don't maintain a 20% close rate, then what I have to do is swap you down to, like, lower priority on the calendar.' Chris adds that if lower priority does not fix it, 'we have to talk about what it would look like past that point, especially now that we're spending money on ads, a lot of these calls are actually costing us money.'
Richard's actual close rate is stated by a third manager: 'when I was having a conversation with Luke, he was like, what's going on with Richard? He's closing at like 11%.'

Deposits are confirmed as routine and as failing at a high rate. Richard: 'then I have a few deposits, they just fall through again... two of them already got canceled. There's only one still open deposit.' Chris counts three. This corroborates the improvised $100-$200 deposits this rep took on both 06/29 calls.

Chris uses outstanding deposits to soften the reported close rate to another manager: 'yeah, but it's like not the whole story because he also has three deposits and yes, we need to get them to become closes, but ultimately it's not as bad as it like seems.' Two of those three had already been cancelled.

A $199 per month price is publicly visible online and is actively anchoring prospects against the $6,000 offer. Richard: 'And I was expecting $199 a month. So he saw it online... if someone sees already, like, it's $199... then they don't want to do that because they want what I talked about.' Chris confirms the source — 'Yeah, it's because of school' — and advises 'I wouldn't worry about it too much.' This is the mechanism behind the same rep pivoting two prospects in this period onto a $200/month community product.

Chris states a clear affordability ethic and declines to push a marginal sale: 'based off the context you gave me, that he's living off savings, he's got kids to feed, he's barely making any money... I don't think I would push this guy to close either. I don't think it would be best for him.' Richard agrees: 'I don't want to put him in a financial bad position.' This is the stated norm against which the 06/29 call, where the same rep pressed an overdrawn prospect for a same-day deposit, should be read as a deviation.

Chris models injury-recovery claims for reps to use, including a hedge that does not appear on this rep's live calls: 'We've had a lot of clients that we've worked with who've been able to completely, fully recover from a lot of the things that you're noticing. I can't say I can promise it for sure, but ultimately, it's happened quite a lot.'

A second consecutive coaching session about selling to prospects with back and knee injuries contains no mention of clinical screening, contraindications, physician clearance, or any circumstance in which a sale should be refused on medical grounds.

Stated policy on call outcomes: 'I don't leave the call on a think-about-it. I don't leave the call on anything that isn't a clear yes or a clear no.' Chris frames the only acceptable endings as a resolved financial yes or no, or a recognised and decided fear.

Richard admits repeating language he did not understand, copied from another rep's recordings: 'I think I saw it in one of Andrew's calls, but he, of course, had context around it. I didn't, but I just said it because I sort of heard him say it once.' Chris corrects him: 'If you don't have the full context of why someone is saying something... then you shouldn't say it.'
The third pillar is formally renamed during the session: 'Change support and accountability to lifelong success and talk about the fact that we're going to set them up for the long-term.'

Chris instructs Richard to abandon the pitch document on his next call: 'Next call, do not show up with any script of whatever... Pillar one, you need to fill in the information yourself on selling up the transformation.'
A separate lost prospect resurfaced after a no-show and cited a family circumstance involving his child's stepfather; he remains interested but not now.
